title: van der Waals grain boundaries with inert electrical behaviors in inorganic molecular dielectric film

paper_content.abstract: Grain boundaries (GBs) in insulating crystal films generally create lattice reconstruction and excess mid-gap states, which may form the transport pathways of charge carriers and lead to serious degradation of insulating properties. Here, we reveal the inert electrical behaviors of GBs in polycrystalline inorganic molecular dielectric film attributed to its special van der Waals structure. Temperature-dependent electrical measurements and first-principles calculations uncovered that such GBs are free of mid-gap states, which explains the unexpectedly low leakage current of Sb2O3 polycrystalline thin film. Through systematic measurements by conductive atomic force microscopy, we further verify the undistinguishable electrical behaviors within grains and at GBs of the polycrystalline film. Our findings may lay a solid foundation for the applications of inorganic molecular film as a compatible gate dielectric in advanced two-dimensional devices.
paper_content.introduction:
Insulating crystals with van der Waals (vdW) surface, such as hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) are gaining increasing attention for their superior performance as gate dielectrics, which facilitates the research in solid-state physics1–7 and integrated devices based on two-dimensional (2D) materials8–10. When integrated with 2D materials, they can form a well-saturated interface and enable the fabrication of high-performance devices such as field-effect transistors (FETs). However, most reported vdW insulating crystals with layered structure are integrated with 2D materials via the exfoliation-and-transfer method, incompatible with the semiconductor manufacturing processes11–17. A new type of vdW insulating crystal, antimony trioxide (Sb2O3) with a caged inorganic molecular structure, known as an inorganic molecular crystal (IMC), emerged and attracted plenty of research interests18–28. Apart from its excellent performance in 2D devices, it can be fabricated via thermal sublimation process. This foundry-compatible fabrication technique offers unparalleled convenience for the scalable integration of 2D circuits18,19. A puzzling fact, however, remains unexplained for this inorganic molecular dielectric film. A polycrystalline film usually possesses far inferior properties to its single-crystalline counterpart due to the presence of grain boundaries (GBs). For instance, GBs in insulators can create reconstructed lattice bonds and excess mid-gap states, which may act as charge carrier pathways and lead to serious degradation of their insulating performance29–37. Contrary to this classic theory, the fabricated polycrystalline inorganic molecular film (PIMF) of Sb2O3 with nanometer-scale grains exhibits an unexpectedly high insulating property18.

In this work, we present theoretical and experimental results on the electrical behaviors of Sb2O3 PIMF. The common GBs in conventional dielectric crystals can result in lattice reconstruction and excess mid-gap states, which form leakage pathways of charge carriers and degrade the insulating performance (Fig. 1a). We show, in contrast, that the excellent insulating properties of PIMF arise from the inert electrical behaviors of its GBs with a typical vdW structure. The saturated vdW GBs are free of mid-gap states, resulting in almost identical insulating properties of polycrystalline film and its single-crystal counterpart (Fig. 1b).
paper_content.results:
Fabrication of PIMF and electrical measurements
The PIMF of Sb2O3 can be fabricated via a thermal sublimation evaporation deposition method18,20. The deposited molecules remain in the cage-like structure and grow into a polycrystalline film on any given substrate, as illustrated in Fig. 2a. We first demonstrate the polycrystalline structure of the Sb2O3 film with a thickness of 10 nm grown on substrates of few-layer graphene (see Methods for details). This is the minimum thickness necessary to prevent the direct tunneling of charges18. As shown in Fig. 2b, the selected area electron diffraction (SAED) pattern confirms the single-crystalline nature of the underlying graphene, whereas the multi-oriented Sb2O3 domains give rise to grain size of around 9.6 nm (see Figure S1), close to the film thickness of 10 nm. This result implies that there may exist high-density transverse GBs (crossing from the top of the film to the bottom) within the film. For electrical characterizations, the Sb2O3 film was directly on a degenerately doped Si substrate, which serves as a flat bottom electrode. We tried to observe the Sb2O3 grains GBs from the cross-section HR-TEM image (Fig. 2d). We can clearly identify the Sb2O3 grains as well as the transverse GBs. Such an insulating film with a large number of continuous pathways for charge carrier transport is theoretically expected to possess a poor current-blocking property. In contrast, it exhibits a low leakage current in our device measurements at room temperature using a parallel plate capacitor (Figure S2). The current density (J) as a function of electric field (E) is furthermore investigated at various temperatures (Fig. 2e). We estimate that each device contains over 108 grains on average between the two electrodes with an area of 200 μm × 200 μm. Despite the presence of such high-density GBs, the measured leakage current density remains as low as 10−7 A/cm2 at an electrical field of 2 MV/cm. Moreover, as we can see in Fig. 2e, the measured leakage current density at varying electric field is independent of temperature. We analyze the electrical properties using Fowler-Nordheim tunneling (FNT) theory for a 10 nm thick insulating film at high electric field. The current density J and bias voltage V can be related using the following equation38–41:

ln(J/V2) = ln(q3m/8πhФB d2m*) - (8π(2m*)1/2 ФB3/2 d / 3hqV) (1)

where m and m* are electron mass and effective electron mass, q is electron charge, ФB is energy barrier, d is the thickness of the insulating layer. The strong linearity between ln(J(V))/V2 and 1/V can be identified from the plots (Fig. 4e inset), and they also exhibit clear independence on temperature, which is in good agreement with FNT theory. For an insulating layer with mid-gap states, the tunneling current generally follows the defect-assisted or trap-assisted tunneling theories42,43. For instance, the charge carriers tunneling assisted by the trap states located within the insulating layer may follow the Poole-Frenkel emission mechanism42,44,45. Its current density J and bias voltage V are related as:

ln(J(V)) / V ~ 1/V1/2 + 1/kT (2)

where kb is the Boltzmann constant and T is the temperature. We can see that for such a mechanism, ln(J(V))/V shows linear relation with V1/2 instead of V and it, moreover, exhibits clear dependence on temperature T45,46. These characteristics are in clear contrast to our measured results (Fig. 2e). Based on such analysis on the electrical transport behaviors, it can be, in turn, confirmed that the tunneling behaviors through our Sb2O3 insulating layer are free of defect- or trap-assisted mechanisms.

Impact of vdW GBs on DOS by calculations
We now try to gain insights into the impact of GBs on the electronic band structure of Sb2O3 crystals. As the molecular structure of Sb2O3 is preserved intact in the sublimation-deposition process, we reasonably assume that all the GBs in Sb2O3 are of vdW structure, as schematically shown in Fig. 2a. In order to investigate the impact of such GB presence on the insulating properties, we performed first-principles calculations to study the band structure of the Sb2O3 polycrystalline film (see details in supplementary materials). We constructed several typical crystal models with low-index crystal planes of (100), (110), (111), and (210), which have the lowest formation energy. A large enough vacuum layer is constructed to create the surface. In these crystal models, the complete molecular structure of Sb2O3 is maintained on the exposed surfaces (Fig. 3a). Since the possible excess mid-gap states in polycrystalline film originate from the breakage of the periodic crystal structure at the GBs, the band structure of our crystal models can represent the scenario of polycrystalline film47. Their calculated results of DOS are compared with those of bulk single crystal (Fig. 3b). The results show that they possess exactly the same band gap and introduce no excess mid-gap states for all the constructed crystal models, thanks to the termination of complete molecules. We specifically indicated that the DOS contributed from the top-layer exposed molecules, and all of their electronic states also remain out of the band gap (Fig. 3b). More explicitly, we constructed some representative crystal models containing GBs and investigated their DOS (see details in Supplementary Materials). For a face-centered cubic (FCC) crystal of Sb2O3, Σ3 and Σ5 twin GBs are preferentially formed in experiments due to their relatively low GB formation energies, which are chosen as two typical bi-crystal models for studying the effects of GBs. The Σ3 out-of-plane twist twin boundary (denoted as GB1, Fig. 3c) and the Σ5 in-plane tilt twin boundary (denoted as GB2, Fig. S3) were therefore selected as representative computational models due to their relatively small number of atoms. They can effectively balance computational efficiency and the accurate description of their physical properties. Their crystal structures were optimized, and electronic structures were calculated (Fig. 3d). The two bi-crystal models possess very similar band gap, which is slightly smaller than the bulk crystal calculated via the same approximation method (see detailed analysis in Supplementary Materials). No excess mid-gap states are created despite the presence of GBs. Such theoretical results imply that the presence of vdW GBs in Sb2O3 PIMF will not result in any mid-gap states, in clear contrast to conventional oxide dielectric materials30,31. The PIMF Sb2O3 possesses an identical band gap to the single-crystal film.

Electrical measurement of Grains and GBs in PIMF via C-AFM
To directly investigate the insulating properties of PIMF at GBs, we employ conductive atomic force microscopy (C-AFM) to probe the nanoelectronic properties of Sb2O3 PIMF at the GBs and within the grains (see experimental details in supplementary materials). C-AFM allows for electrical measurements at local positions with nanometer resolution, and the results can be conveniently correlated with the morphology of the sample surface48–51, enabling us to access the electrical behaviors of GBs and grains simultaneously (Fig. 4a). We first obtain the morphology of the PIMF. Thanks to the effect of GB grooving in the film that grows via deposition, we can identify the GBs and grains from the AFM images (Fig. 4b). We then apply ramp voltage stress on specific positions (at GBs or in grains) and carry out the electrical measurements. Figure 4c shows the forward and backwards sweeping E-I curves obtained at GBs and within grains from over 100 positions, with a current limitation of 100 pA to protect the tip and the sample52. Statistically, we find no discernible difference between GBs and grains' E-I curves. The average E-I curves obtained from GBs and grains are almost overlapped (thick curves in Fig. 4c), both for forward and backwards sweeping, which implies an identical electrical property for GBs and grains of our Sb2O3 PIMF. We also analyzed the average E-I curves using FNT theory, as shown in Fig. 4d. Their linear relation implies that both the electrical behaviors of GBs and grains are in good agreement with the FNT as well (analysis of the measured data is shown in Fig. S3). The required electrical field to reach a fixed leakage current of 3 pA for GBs and grains is plotted statically in Fig. 4e, from which we can see that they exhibit very similar values. C-AFM also allows for mapping leakage currents over a given area, which can provide the insulating properties over a continuous area. Applying a constant bias voltage of 3.5 V on the C-AFM tip, the leakage currents in a 500 nm × 500 nm area are mapped for three times (Fig. 4f). As we can observe, most area exhibits an ultra-low conductivity while some regions are more conductive (dark points in Fig. 4f), however, it is clear that such highly-conductive regions do not correlate to the positions of GBs and the position do not repeat in multiple scans; moreover, the currents decrease as the stress proceed due to the presence of charge trapping effect, i.e. some charges get trapped and released from the trapping points. This result is in contrast with multiple observations of enhanced currents and fast degradation at the grain boundaries of metal oxides like HfO253,54. Therefore, this behavior observed in GBs of Sb2O3 PIMF is quite unique and offers higher opportunities for being used as a gate dielectric.
paper_content.methods:
Thermal evaporation deposition of PIMF Sb2O3
The deposition of Sb2O3 was carried out in a standard thermal evaporation deposition system (Nexdep, Angstrom Engineering) in a high vacuum (10−6 torr). Sb2O3 powder was sublimated by heating and deposited on substrates. The deposition rate was precisely controlled by an in-situ quartz crystal oscillator. To maintain the flatness of the obtained Sb2O3 film, the deposition rate in this work was 0.06 Å s−1 for the entire fabrication process.

Sample preparation for TEM characterizations
For plan-view TEM samples, we exfoliated a few-layer graphene flakes onto SiO2/Si substrate and then transferred them onto a TEM grid assisted by a PMMA membrane. Then the PMMA membrane on the TEM grid is dissolved in acetone. Afterwards, the TEM grid with graphene flakes is annealed in an Ar atmosphere to remove the PMMA residues on graphene flakes, which is then loaded into the thermal evaporation deposition system, and Sb2O3 is deposited. For the cross-section TEM lamella, 10 nm of Sb2O3 was deposited onto a degenerately doped silicon substrate, and then the lamella was fabricated by a dual focused ion beam system (Helios Nanolab G3 UC, FEI). TEM images and SAED were obtained using an FEI Tecnai G2 20.

Preparation and characterization of capacitor devices
10 nm of Sb2O3 was deposited onto a degenerately doped silicon substrate. A shadow mask with a predefined size of 200 μm × 200 μm was placed over the film, followed by the deposition of 40 nm of Au via thermal evaporation to form the top metal electrode. In such a way, the devices for electrical characterizations can be maintained free of contamination resulting from the fabrication processes.

Electrical measurements
Current-voltage measurements were performed in a probe station (Lakeshore) equipped with a semiconductor analyzer (Keithley 4200). We pump the chamber and keep it in a high vacuum (10−6 torr) for 3 h to eliminate the gas adsorption on device surfaces before the device test. Afterwards, the device tests are carried out at various temperatures.

Theoretical calculations
The details of the theoretical calculations are described in the Supplementary Materials.

C-AFM characterization
Conductive atomic force microscopy (C-AFM) experiments were carried out on a Bruker Dimension Icon instrument fitted with a Nanoscope VI controller and PFTUNA module. Measurements were performed in ambient air (relative humidity ≈ 54%). Surface topography was mapped in tapping mode using an NCHV-A tip (spring constant 42 N/m), whereas nanoelectronic characterization, including current mapping and I–V spectroscopy, was obtained in PF-TUNA (tunneling current) mode with a solid platinum RNM25PT300B probe (spring constant 18 N/m). Imaging scans were acquired at 1 Hz, and all I–V curves were collected under a compliance current of 100 pA to prevent damage to both tip and sample. The onset potential (VON) was defined as the voltage at which the measured current first exceeded the system noise level (≈ 3 pA).

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The authors investigated the insulating properties of Sb2O3 polycrystalline inorganic molecular film while paid particular
attentions to its grain boundaries. This kind of film attract research interests recently for its great potentials as a decent van
der Waals dielectric film in advanced 2D-semiconductor-based devices, which can be conveniently fabricated and
integrated in a scalable way. A polycrystalline film is expected to have poor insulating properties in theory since the grain
boundaries as typical crystal defects can form the leakage paths. However, in this work, the authors revealed that the grain
boundaries in Sb2O3 polycrystalline film with van der Waals structure create no defects. They provided robust evidences of
device measurements and theoretical calculations and explain a puzzling fact: why Sb2O3 polycrystalline film possesses an
excellent current-blocking property. This work is of significance for applications of this promising dielectric material in future
2D integrated circuits. I recommend it be accepted for publication in Nature Communications after my concerns as follows
are well addressed.
1.In Fig.1a, the schematic figure depicting defect-assisted tunneling is probably incorrect. The charge carriers are supposed
to hop between defect states via emission mechanism instead of tunneling. The leakage current is temperature-dependent
only via emission mechanism in theory. The authors should reconsider the mechanism, correct the figure and the related
content in the manuscript.
2.The standard of leakage current for a gate dielectric (DRAM for instance) should be marked in Fig.2e so that the insulating
performance of Sb2O3 film can be clearly identified.
3.In the current mappings Fig.4 f, there are some points that show high leakage current. What has caused this leakage?
4.As we know, the dielectric materials used in many organic devices are made of organic molecules. Is the conclusion also
applicable to organic molecular dielectric materials? I think it would be interesting if this phenomenon can be extended to
organic molecular dielectric materials and added relevant content in the part of Discussion.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The manuscript by Liu et al. reports an intriguing observation that the grain boundaries (GBs) of Sb₂O₃ do not exhibit
leakage current, in stark contrast to conventional insulating films such as HfO₂. The authors attribute this behavior to the
intrinsic van der Waals (vdW) structure of Sb₂O₃, which purportedly suppresses the formation of charge transport pathways
via mid-gap states at the GBs. If validated, this could have substantial implications for the future design of dielectric materials
in next-generation electronic devices.
However, I believe that further clarification is required to disentangle the effects of the Sb₂O₃ material itself from those
potentially introduced by the graphene layers used in the experiments. I raise the following concerns:
1. The suppression of leakage current might not be solely due to the intrinsic properties of Sb₂O₃. As noted on page 3,
multiple layers of graphene were intentionally inserted to block direct tunneling of charge carriers. It is therefore critical to
clarify whether the absence of leakage at GBs is a result of the Sb₂O₃ properties alone or whether it is influenced—partially
or substantially—by the presence of graphene. The authors should provide a clear explanation or experimental evidence
ruling out the contribution of graphene to the observed leakage suppression.
2. Related to the above point, Figure 2d is said to show the cross-sectional TEM image, but it is unclear whether the multiple
graphene layers are visible or identifiable in this image. If graphene is indeed present, it should be explicitly marked or
referenced, and the number of layers should be specified.
3. It is also unclear whether the measurements presented in Figure 4 were performed on structures that include the
graphene layers. Since graphene may strongly influence the electronic properties, especially near GBs, this information is
essential. If graphene is present in these measurements, it should be consistently annotated throughout the figures and text.
The current description only briefly mentions graphene on page 3, with no further indication of its presence in subsequent
experiments, which could lead to misunderstandings about the experimental conditions.
4. On page 7, the authors state: “We first obtain the morphology of the PIMF, from which the GBs and grains can be identified
(Figure 4b).” However, Figure 4b does not appear to show atomic-resolution imaging, which casts doubt on whether the
features identified can be definitively assigned as grain boundaries. The authors should clarify the resolution of this image
and discuss any supporting evidence that validates the interpretation of the observed features as GBs.
In summary, while the results are promising, I recommend that the authors provide more detailed and unambiguous
evidence to isolate the intrinsic effects of Sb₂O₃ from potential contributions of the graphene interlayers. Without this
clarification, the claim that Sb₂O₃ GBs intrinsically suppress leakage remains open to alternative interpretations.
Minor comment: The abbreviation IMC appears in the manuscript but is not defined upon first usage. The authors are
advised to ensure that all abbreviations, including IMC and others throughout the text, are clearly defined when first
introduced for clarity.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Kailang Liu et al. study leakage currents across polycrystalline dielectric films deposited by thermal evaporation of Sb₂O₃.
While the basic dielectric properties of these films, including dielectric permittivity and leakage current, were previously
characterized by the authors [Nature Electronics 4, 906–913 (2021)], they show here that the leakage currents are fairly
uniform across both grain interiors and grain boundaries (GBs), and they attribute this uniformity to the absence of mid-gap
states at GBs. My specific comments are below.
1. The dielectric film exhibits decent insulating properties, with a low leakage current of ~10⁻⁷ A/cm² at a thickness of 10 nm
(equivalent oxide thickness ~3.5 nm). However, although the authors compare their results with HfO₂—where GBs are
known to introduce mid-gap states and enable defect-assisted tunneling—the advantage of Sb₂O₃ remains somewhat
unclear. Reported leakage currents for HfO₂ at similar EOTs are comparable, despite its polycrystallinity. What is the
leakage current of the Sb₂O₃ dielectric at sub-1 nm EOT for state-of-the-art MOSFETs? The authors should clarify the
significance of their films as gate dielectrics.
2. The grain size in Fig. 4 (a few tens of nanometers) is too small to fully isolate current through GBs from that through grain
interiors using C-AFM in ambient conditions. Measurements on samples with much larger grains (>~100 nm) would be
required for a proper comparison, given the spatial resolution of C-AFM and the film thickness.
3. Do the deposited dielectric films retain the pristine caged inorganic molecular structures proposed in the schematics (Fig.
2a)? In particular, after thermal deposition, the individual Sb₂O₃ molecules could contain various atomic defects (e.g.,
vacancies) or form polymeric chains with different stoichiometries. If such atomic defects are uniformly present and govern
the leakage current level, GB-specific effects would be difficult to observe.
4. In Fig. 3, the results show changes in electronic states associated with different crystalline surfaces only. To assess GB
effects, simulations should be performed on structures that explicitly contain a GB, where two different crystalline domains
are interfaced.
5. In Fig. 4f, the locations of high-leakage spots change as the scan is repeated, suggesting structural evolution of the
dielectric during measurement. What is the structural origin of these local high-leakage currents, and why do their positions
shift during repeated scans?

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Grain boundaries (GBs) in insulating crystal films generally create lattice reconstruction and excess mid-gap states, which may form the transport pathways of charge carriers and lead to serious degradation of insulating properties. Here, we reveal the inert electrical behaviors of GBs in polycrystalline inorganic molecular dielectric film attributed to its special van der Waals structure. Temperature-dependent electrical measurements and first-principles calculations uncovered that such GBs are free of mid-gap states, which explains the unexpectedly low leakage current of Sb2O3 polycrystalline thin film. Through systematic measurements by conductive atomic force microscopy, we further verify the undistinguishable electrical behaviors within grains and at GBs of the polycrystalline film. Our findings may lay a solid foundation for the applications of inorganic molecular film as a compatible gate dielectric in advanced two-dimensional devices.

---

## Introduction

Insulating crystals with van der Waals (vdW) surface, such as hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) are gaining increasing attention for their superior performance as gate dielectrics, which facilitates the research in solid-state physics1–7 and integrated devices based on two-dimensional (2D) materials8–10. When integrated with 2D materials, they can form a well-saturated interface and enable the fabrication of high-performance devices such as field-effect transistors (FETs). However, most reported vdW insulating crystals with layered structure are integrated with 2D materials via the exfoliation-and-transfer method, incompatible with the semiconductor manufacturing processes11–17. A new type of vdW insulating crystal, antimony trioxide (Sb2O3) with a caged inorganic molecular structure, known as an inorganic molecular crystal (IMC), emerged and attracted plenty of research interests18–28. Apart from its excellent performance in 2D devices, it can be fabricated via thermal sublimation process. This foundry-compatible fabrication technique offers unparalleled convenience for the scalable integration of 2D circuits18,19. A puzzling fact, however, remains unexplained for this inorganic molecular dielectric film. A polycrystalline film usually possesses far inferior properties to its single-crystalline counterpart due to the presence of grain boundaries (GBs). For instance, GBs in insulators can create reconstructed lattice bonds and excess mid-gap states, which may act as charge carrier pathways and lead to serious degradation of their insulating performance29–37. Contrary to this classic theory, the fabricated polycrystalline inorganic molecular film (PIMF) of Sb2O3 with nanometer-scale grains exhibits an unexpectedly high insulating property18.

In this work, we present theoretical and experimental results on the electrical behaviors of Sb2O3 PIMF. The common GBs in conventional dielectric crystals can result in lattice reconstruction and excess mid-gap states, which form leakage pathways of charge carriers and degrade the insulating performance (Fig. 1a). We show, in contrast, that the excellent insulating properties of PIMF arise from the inert electrical behaviors of its GBs with a typical vdW structure. The saturated vdW GBs are free of mid-gap states, resulting in almost identical insulating properties of polycrystalline film and its single-crystal counterpart (Fig. 1b).

---

## Results

Fabrication of PIMF and electrical measurements
The PIMF of Sb2O3 can be fabricated via a thermal sublimation evaporation deposition method18,20. The deposited molecules remain in the cage-like structure and grow into a polycrystalline film on any given substrate, as illustrated in Fig. 2a. We first demonstrate the polycrystalline structure of the Sb2O3 film with a thickness of 10 nm grown on substrates of few-layer graphene (see Methods for details). This is the minimum thickness necessary to prevent the direct tunneling of charges18. As shown in Fig. 2b, the selected area electron diffraction (SAED) pattern confirms the single-crystalline nature of the underlying graphene, whereas the multi-oriented Sb2O3 domains give rise to grain size of around 9.6 nm (see Figure S1), close to the film thickness of 10 nm. This result implies that there may exist high-density transverse GBs (crossing from the top of the film to the bottom) within the film. For electrical characterizations, the Sb2O3 film was directly on a degenerately doped Si substrate, which serves as a flat bottom electrode. We tried to observe the Sb2O3 grains GBs from the cross-section HR-TEM image (Fig. 2d). We can clearly identify the Sb2O3 grains as well as the transverse GBs. Such an insulating film with a large number of continuous pathways for charge carrier transport is theoretically expected to possess a poor current-blocking property. In contrast, it exhibits a low leakage current in our device measurements at room temperature using a parallel plate capacitor (Figure S2). The current density (J) as a function of electric field (E) is furthermore investigated at various temperatures (Fig. 2e). We estimate that each device contains over 108 grains on average between the two electrodes with an area of 200 μm × 200 μm. Despite the presence of such high-density GBs, the measured leakage current density remains as low as 10−7 A/cm2 at an electrical field of 2 MV/cm. Moreover, as we can see in Fig. 2e, the measured leakage current density at varying electric field is independent of temperature. We analyze the electrical properties using Fowler-Nordheim tunneling (FNT) theory for a 10 nm thick insulating film at high electric field. The current density J and bias voltage V can be related using the following equation38–41:

ln(J/V2) = ln(q3m/8πhФB d2m*) - (8π(2m*)1/2 ФB3/2 d / 3hqV) (1)

where m and m* are electron mass and effective electron mass, q is electron charge, ФB is energy barrier, d is the thickness of the insulating layer. The strong linearity between ln(J(V))/V2 and 1/V can be identified from the plots (Fig. 4e inset), and they also exhibit clear independence on temperature, which is in good agreement with FNT theory. For an insulating layer with mid-gap states, the tunneling current generally follows the defect-assisted or trap-assisted tunneling theories42,43. For instance, the charge carriers tunneling assisted by the trap states located within the insulating layer may follow the Poole-Frenkel emission mechanism42,44,45. Its current density J and bias voltage V are related as:

ln(J(V)) / V ~ 1/V1/2 + 1/kT (2)

where kb is the Boltzmann constant and T is the temperature. We can see that for such a mechanism, ln(J(V))/V shows linear relation with V1/2 instead of V and it, moreover, exhibits clear dependence on temperature T45,46. These characteristics are in clear contrast to our measured results (Fig. 2e). Based on such analysis on the electrical transport behaviors, it can be, in turn, confirmed that the tunneling behaviors through our Sb2O3 insulating layer are free of defect- or trap-assisted mechanisms.

Impact of vdW GBs on DOS by calculations
We now try to gain insights into the impact of GBs on the electronic band structure of Sb2O3 crystals. As the molecular structure of Sb2O3 is preserved intact in the sublimation-deposition process, we reasonably assume that all the GBs in Sb2O3 are of vdW structure, as schematically shown in Fig. 2a. In order to investigate the impact of such GB presence on the insulating properties, we performed first-principles calculations to study the band structure of the Sb2O3 polycrystalline film (see details in supplementary materials). We constructed several typical crystal models with low-index crystal planes of (100), (110), (111), and (210), which have the lowest formation energy. A large enough vacuum layer is constructed to create the surface. In these crystal models, the complete molecular structure of Sb2O3 is maintained on the exposed surfaces (Fig. 3a). Since the possible excess mid-gap states in polycrystalline film originate from the breakage of the periodic crystal structure at the GBs, the band structure of our crystal models can represent the scenario of polycrystalline film47. Their calculated results of DOS are compared with those of bulk single crystal (Fig. 3b). The results show that they possess exactly the same band gap and introduce no excess mid-gap states for all the constructed crystal models, thanks to the termination of complete molecules. We specifically indicated that the DOS contributed from the top-layer exposed molecules, and all of their electronic states also remain out of the band gap (Fig. 3b). More explicitly, we constructed some representative crystal models containing GBs and investigated their DOS (see details in Supplementary Materials). For a face-centered cubic (FCC) crystal of Sb2O3, Σ3 and Σ5 twin GBs are preferentially formed in experiments due to their relatively low GB formation energies, which are chosen as two typical bi-crystal models for studying the effects of GBs. The Σ3 out-of-plane twist twin boundary (denoted as GB1, Fig. 3c) and the Σ5 in-plane tilt twin boundary (denoted as GB2, Fig. S3) were therefore selected as representative computational models due to their relatively small number of atoms. They can effectively balance computational efficiency and the accurate description of their physical properties. Their crystal structures were optimized, and electronic structures were calculated (Fig. 3d). The two bi-crystal models possess very similar band gap, which is slightly smaller than the bulk crystal calculated via the same approximation method (see detailed analysis in Supplementary Materials). No excess mid-gap states are created despite the presence of GBs. Such theoretical results imply that the presence of vdW GBs in Sb2O3 PIMF will not result in any mid-gap states, in clear contrast to conventional oxide dielectric materials30,31. The PIMF Sb2O3 possesses an identical band gap to the single-crystal film.

Electrical measurement of Grains and GBs in PIMF via C-AFM
To directly investigate the insulating properties of PIMF at GBs, we employ conductive atomic force microscopy (C-AFM) to probe the nanoelectronic properties of Sb2O3 PIMF at the GBs and within the grains (see experimental details in supplementary materials). C-AFM allows for electrical measurements at local positions with nanometer resolution, and the results can be conveniently correlated with the morphology of the sample surface48–51, enabling us to access the electrical behaviors of GBs and grains simultaneously (Fig. 4a). We first obtain the morphology of the PIMF. Thanks to the effect of GB grooving in the film that grows via deposition, we can identify the GBs and grains from the AFM images (Fig. 4b). We then apply ramp voltage stress on specific positions (at GBs or in grains) and carry out the electrical measurements. Figure 4c shows the forward and backwards sweeping E-I curves obtained at GBs and within grains from over 100 positions, with a current limitation of 100 pA to protect the tip and the sample52. Statistically, we find no discernible difference between GBs and grains' E-I curves. The average E-I curves obtained from GBs and grains are almost overlapped (thick curves in Fig. 4c), both for forward and backwards sweeping, which implies an identical electrical property for GBs and grains of our Sb2O3 PIMF. We also analyzed the average E-I curves using FNT theory, as shown in Fig. 4d. Their linear relation implies that both the electrical behaviors of GBs and grains are in good agreement with the FNT as well (analysis of the measured data is shown in Fig. S3). The required electrical field to reach a fixed leakage current of 3 pA for GBs and grains is plotted statically in Fig. 4e, from which we can see that they exhibit very similar values. C-AFM also allows for mapping leakage currents over a given area, which can provide the insulating properties over a continuous area. Applying a constant bias voltage of 3.5 V on the C-AFM tip, the leakage currents in a 500 nm × 500 nm area are mapped for three times (Fig. 4f). As we can observe, most area exhibits an ultra-low conductivity while some regions are more conductive (dark points in Fig. 4f), however, it is clear that such highly-conductive regions do not correlate to the positions of GBs and the position do not repeat in multiple scans; moreover, the currents decrease as the stress proceed due to the presence of charge trapping effect, i.e. some charges get trapped and released from the trapping points. This result is in contrast with multiple observations of enhanced currents and fast degradation at the grain boundaries of metal oxides like HfO253,54. Therefore, this behavior observed in GBs of Sb2O3 PIMF is quite unique and offers higher opportunities for being used as a gate dielectric.

---

## Methods

Thermal evaporation deposition of PIMF Sb2O3
The deposition of Sb2O3 was carried out in a standard thermal evaporation deposition system (Nexdep, Angstrom Engineering) in a high vacuum (10−6 torr). Sb2O3 powder was sublimated by heating and deposited on substrates. The deposition rate was precisely controlled by an in-situ quartz crystal oscillator. To maintain the flatness of the obtained Sb2O3 film, the deposition rate in this work was 0.06 Å s−1 for the entire fabrication process.

Sample preparation for TEM characterizations
For plan-view TEM samples, we exfoliated a few-layer graphene flakes onto SiO2/Si substrate and then transferred them onto a TEM grid assisted by a PMMA membrane. Then the PMMA membrane on the TEM grid is dissolved in acetone. Afterwards, the TEM grid with graphene flakes is annealed in an Ar atmosphere to remove the PMMA residues on graphene flakes, which is then loaded into the thermal evaporation deposition system, and Sb2O3 is deposited. For the cross-section TEM lamella, 10 nm of Sb2O3 was deposited onto a degenerately doped silicon substrate, and then the lamella was fabricated by a dual focused ion beam system (Helios Nanolab G3 UC, FEI). TEM images and SAED were obtained using an FEI Tecnai G2 20.

Preparation and characterization of capacitor devices
10 nm of Sb2O3 was deposited onto a degenerately doped silicon substrate. A shadow mask with a predefined size of 200 μm × 200 μm was placed over the film, followed by the deposition of 40 nm of Au via thermal evaporation to form the top metal electrode. In such a way, the devices for electrical characterizations can be maintained free of contamination resulting from the fabrication processes.

Electrical measurements
Current-voltage measurements were performed in a probe station (Lakeshore) equipped with a semiconductor analyzer (Keithley 4200). We pump the chamber and keep it in a high vacuum (10−6 torr) for 3 h to eliminate the gas adsorption on device surfaces before the device test. Afterwards, the device tests are carried out at various temperatures.

Theoretical calculations
The details of the theoretical calculations are described in the Supplementary Materials.

C-AFM characterization
Conductive atomic force microscopy (C-AFM) experiments were carried out on a Bruker Dimension Icon instrument fitted with a Nanoscope VI controller and PFTUNA module. Measurements were performed in ambient air (relative humidity ≈ 54%). Surface topography was mapped in tapping mode using an NCHV-A tip (spring constant 42 N/m), whereas nanoelectronic characterization, including current mapping and I–V spectroscopy, was obtained in PF-TUNA (tunneling current) mode with a solid platinum RNM25PT300B probe (spring constant 18 N/m). Imaging scans were acquired at 1 Hz, and all I–V curves were collected under a compliance current of 100 pA to prevent damage to both tip and sample. The onset potential (VON) was defined as the voltage at which the measured current first exceeded the system noise level (≈ 3 pA).

## Paper

## Abstract

Grain boundaries (GBs) in insulating crystal films generally create lattice reconstruction and excess mid-gap states, which may form the transport pathways of charge carriers and lead to serious degradation of insulating properties. Here, we reveal the inert electrical behaviors of GBs in polycrystalline inorganic molecular dielectric film attributed to its special van der Waals structure. Temperature-dependent electrical measurements and first-principles calculations uncovered that such GBs are free of mid-gap states, which explains the unexpectedly low leakage current of Sb2O3 polycrystalline thin film. Through systematic measurements by conductive atomic force microscopy, we further verify the undistinguishable electrical behaviors within grains and at GBs of the polycrystalline film. Our findings may lay a solid foundation for the applications of inorganic molecular film as a compatible gate dielectric in advanced two-dimensional devices.

---

## Introduction

Insulating crystals with van der Waals (vdW) surface, such as hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) are gaining increasing attention for their superior performance as gate dielectrics, which facilitates the research in solid-state physics1–7 and integrated devices based on two-dimensional (2D) materials8–10. When integrated with 2D materials, they can form a well-saturated interface and enable the fabrication of high-performance devices such as field-effect transistors (FETs). However, most reported vdW insulating crystals with layered structure are integrated with 2D materials via the exfoliation-and-transfer method, incompatible with the semiconductor manufacturing processes11–17. A new type of vdW insulating crystal, antimony trioxide (Sb2O3) with a caged inorganic molecular structure, known as an inorganic molecular crystal (IMC), emerged and attracted plenty of research interests18–28. Apart from its excellent performance in 2D devices, it can be fabricated via thermal sublimation process. This foundry-compatible fabrication technique offers unparalleled convenience for the scalable integration of 2D circuits18,19. A puzzling fact, however, remains unexplained for this inorganic molecular dielectric film. A polycrystalline film usually possesses far inferior properties to its single-crystalline counterpart due to the presence of grain boundaries (GBs). For instance, GBs in insulators can create reconstructed lattice bonds and excess mid-gap states, which may act as charge carrier pathways and lead to serious degradation of their insulating performance29–37. Contrary to this classic theory, the fabricated polycrystalline inorganic molecular film (PIMF) of Sb2O3 with nanometer-scale grains exhibits an unexpectedly high insulating property18.

In this work, we present theoretical and experimental results on the electrical behaviors of Sb2O3 PIMF. The common GBs in conventional dielectric crystals can result in lattice reconstruction and excess mid-gap states, which form leakage pathways of charge carriers and degrade the insulating performance (Fig. 1a). We show, in contrast, that the excellent insulating properties of PIMF arise from the inert electrical behaviors of its GBs with a typical vdW structure. The saturated vdW GBs are free of mid-gap states, resulting in almost identical insulating properties of polycrystalline film and its single-crystal counterpart (Fig. 1b).

---

## Results

Fabrication of PIMF and electrical measurements
The PIMF of Sb2O3 can be fabricated via a thermal sublimation evaporation deposition method18,20. The deposited molecules remain in the cage-like structure and grow into a polycrystalline film on any given substrate, as illustrated in Fig. 2a. We first demonstrate the polycrystalline structure of the Sb2O3 film with a thickness of 10 nm grown on substrates of few-layer graphene (see Methods for details). This is the minimum thickness necessary to prevent the direct tunneling of charges18. As shown in Fig. 2b, the selected area electron diffraction (SAED) pattern confirms the single-crystalline nature of the underlying graphene, whereas the multi-oriented Sb2O3 domains give rise to grain size of around 9.6 nm (see Figure S1), close to the film thickness of 10 nm. This result implies that there may exist high-density transverse GBs (crossing from the top of the film to the bottom) within the film. For electrical characterizations, the Sb2O3 film was directly on a degenerately doped Si substrate, which serves as a flat bottom electrode. We tried to observe the Sb2O3 grains GBs from the cross-section HR-TEM image (Fig. 2d). We can clearly identify the Sb2O3 grains as well as the transverse GBs. Such an insulating film with a large number of continuous pathways for charge carrier transport is theoretically expected to possess a poor current-blocking property. In contrast, it exhibits a low leakage current in our device measurements at room temperature using a parallel plate capacitor (Figure S2). The current density (J) as a function of electric field (E) is furthermore investigated at various temperatures (Fig. 2e). We estimate that each device contains over 108 grains on average between the two electrodes with an area of 200 μm × 200 μm. Despite the presence of such high-density GBs, the measured leakage current density remains as low as 10−7 A/cm2 at an electrical field of 2 MV/cm. Moreover, as we can see in Fig. 2e, the measured leakage current density at varying electric field is independent of temperature. We analyze the electrical properties using Fowler-Nordheim tunneling (FNT) theory for a 10 nm thick insulating film at high electric field. The current density J and bias voltage V can be related using the following equation38–41:

ln(J/V2) = ln(q3m/8πhФB d2m*) - (8π(2m*)1/2 ФB3/2 d / 3hqV) (1)

where m and m* are electron mass and effective electron mass, q is electron charge, ФB is energy barrier, d is the thickness of the insulating layer. The strong linearity between ln(J(V))/V2 and 1/V can be identified from the plots (Fig. 4e inset), and they also exhibit clear independence on temperature, which is in good agreement with FNT theory. For an insulating layer with mid-gap states, the tunneling current generally follows the defect-assisted or trap-assisted tunneling theories42,43. For instance, the charge carriers tunneling assisted by the trap states located within the insulating layer may follow the Poole-Frenkel emission mechanism42,44,45. Its current density J and bias voltage V are related as:

ln(J(V)) / V ~ 1/V1/2 + 1/kT (2)

where kb is the Boltzmann constant and T is the temperature. We can see that for such a mechanism, ln(J(V))/V shows linear relation with V1/2 instead of V and it, moreover, exhibits clear dependence on temperature T45,46. These characteristics are in clear contrast to our measured results (Fig. 2e). Based on such analysis on the electrical transport behaviors, it can be, in turn, confirmed that the tunneling behaviors through our Sb2O3 insulating layer are free of defect- or trap-assisted mechanisms.

Impact of vdW GBs on DOS by calculations
We now try to gain insights into the impact of GBs on the electronic band structure of Sb2O3 crystals. As the molecular structure of Sb2O3 is preserved intact in the sublimation-deposition process, we reasonably assume that all the GBs in Sb2O3 are of vdW structure, as schematically shown in Fig. 2a. In order to investigate the impact of such GB presence on the insulating properties, we performed first-principles calculations to study the band structure of the Sb2O3 polycrystalline film (see details in supplementary materials). We constructed several typical crystal models with low-index crystal planes of (100), (110), (111), and (210), which have the lowest formation energy. A large enough vacuum layer is constructed to create the surface. In these crystal models, the complete molecular structure of Sb2O3 is maintained on the exposed surfaces (Fig. 3a). Since the possible excess mid-gap states in polycrystalline film originate from the breakage of the periodic crystal structure at the GBs, the band structure of our crystal models can represent the scenario of polycrystalline film47. Their calculated results of DOS are compared with those of bulk single crystal (Fig. 3b). The results show that they possess exactly the same band gap and introduce no excess mid-gap states for all the constructed crystal models, thanks to the termination of complete molecules. We specifically indicated that the DOS contributed from the top-layer exposed molecules, and all of their electronic states also remain out of the band gap (Fig. 3b). More explicitly, we constructed some representative crystal models containing GBs and investigated their DOS (see details in Supplementary Materials). For a face-centered cubic (FCC) crystal of Sb2O3, Σ3 and Σ5 twin GBs are preferentially formed in experiments due to their relatively low GB formation energies, which are chosen as two typical bi-crystal models for studying the effects of GBs. The Σ3 out-of-plane twist twin boundary (denoted as GB1, Fig. 3c) and the Σ5 in-plane tilt twin boundary (denoted as GB2, Fig. S3) were therefore selected as representative computational models due to their relatively small number of atoms. They can effectively balance computational efficiency and the accurate description of their physical properties. Their crystal structures were optimized, and electronic structures were calculated (Fig. 3d). The two bi-crystal models possess very similar band gap, which is slightly smaller than the bulk crystal calculated via the same approximation method (see detailed analysis in Supplementary Materials). No excess mid-gap states are created despite the presence of GBs. Such theoretical results imply that the presence of vdW GBs in Sb2O3 PIMF will not result in any mid-gap states, in clear contrast to conventional oxide dielectric materials30,31. The PIMF Sb2O3 possesses an identical band gap to the single-crystal film.

Electrical measurement of Grains and GBs in PIMF via C-AFM
To directly investigate the insulating properties of PIMF at GBs, we employ conductive atomic force microscopy (C-AFM) to probe the nanoelectronic properties of Sb2O3 PIMF at the GBs and within the grains (see experimental details in supplementary materials). C-AFM allows for electrical measurements at local positions with nanometer resolution, and the results can be conveniently correlated with the morphology of the sample surface48–51, enabling us to access the electrical behaviors of GBs and grains simultaneously (Fig. 4a). We first obtain the morphology of the PIMF. Thanks to the effect of GB grooving in the film that grows via deposition, we can identify the GBs and grains from the AFM images (Fig. 4b). We then apply ramp voltage stress on specific positions (at GBs or in grains) and carry out the electrical measurements. Figure 4c shows the forward and backwards sweeping E-I curves obtained at GBs and within grains from over 100 positions, with a current limitation of 100 pA to protect the tip and the sample52. Statistically, we find no discernible difference between GBs and grains' E-I curves. The average E-I curves obtained from GBs and grains are almost overlapped (thick curves in Fig. 4c), both for forward and backwards sweeping, which implies an identical electrical property for GBs and grains of our Sb2O3 PIMF. We also analyzed the average E-I curves using FNT theory, as shown in Fig. 4d. Their linear relation implies that both the electrical behaviors of GBs and grains are in good agreement with the FNT as well (analysis of the measured data is shown in Fig. S3). The required electrical field to reach a fixed leakage current of 3 pA for GBs and grains is plotted statically in Fig. 4e, from which we can see that they exhibit very similar values. C-AFM also allows for mapping leakage currents over a given area, which can provide the insulating properties over a continuous area. Applying a constant bias voltage of 3.5 V on the C-AFM tip, the leakage currents in a 500 nm × 500 nm area are mapped for three times (Fig. 4f). As we can observe, most area exhibits an ultra-low conductivity while some regions are more conductive (dark points in Fig. 4f), however, it is clear that such highly-conductive regions do not correlate to the positions of GBs and the position do not repeat in multiple scans; moreover, the currents decrease as the stress proceed due to the presence of charge trapping effect, i.e. some charges get trapped and released from the trapping points. This result is in contrast with multiple observations of enhanced currents and fast degradation at the grain boundaries of metal oxides like HfO253,54. Therefore, this behavior observed in GBs of Sb2O3 PIMF is quite unique and offers higher opportunities for being used as a gate dielectric.

## Methods

Thermal evaporation deposition of PIMF Sb2O3
The deposition of Sb2O3 was carried out in a standard thermal evaporation deposition system (Nexdep, Angstrom Engineering) in a high vacuum (10−6 torr). Sb2O3 powder was sublimated by heating and deposited on substrates. The deposition rate was precisely controlled by an in-situ quartz crystal oscillator. To maintain the flatness of the obtained Sb2O3 film, the deposition rate in this work was 0.06 Å s−1 for the entire fabrication process.

Sample preparation for TEM characterizations
For plan-view TEM samples, we exfoliated a few-layer graphene flakes onto SiO2/Si substrate and then transferred them onto a TEM grid assisted by a PMMA membrane. Then the PMMA membrane on the TEM grid is dissolved in acetone. Afterwards, the TEM grid with graphene flakes is annealed in an Ar atmosphere to remove the PMMA residues on graphene flakes, which is then loaded into the thermal evaporation deposition system, and Sb2O3 is deposited. For the cross-section TEM lamella, 10 nm of Sb2O3 was deposited onto a degenerately doped silicon substrate, and then the lamella was fabricated by a dual focused ion beam system (Helios Nanolab G3 UC, FEI). TEM images and SAED were obtained using an FEI Tecnai G2 20.

Preparation and characterization of capacitor devices
10 nm of Sb2O3 was deposited onto a degenerately doped silicon substrate. A shadow mask with a predefined size of 200 μm × 200 μm was placed over the film, followed by the deposition of 40 nm of Au via thermal evaporation to form the top metal electrode. In such a way, the devices for electrical characterizations can be maintained free of contamination resulting from the fabrication processes.

Electrical measurements
Current-voltage measurements were performed in a probe station (Lakeshore) equipped with a semiconductor analyzer (Keithley 4200). We pump the chamber and keep it in a high vacuum (10−6 torr) for 3 h to eliminate the gas adsorption on device surfaces before the device test. Afterwards, the device tests are carried out at various temperatures.

Theoretical calculations
The details of the theoretical calculations are described in the Supplementary Materials.

C-AFM characterization
Conductive atomic force microscopy (C-AFM) experiments were carried out on a Bruker Dimension Icon instrument fitted with a Nanoscope VI controller and PFTUNA module. Measurements were performed in ambient air (relative humidity ≈ 54%). Surface topography was mapped in tapping mode using an NCHV-A tip (spring constant 42 N/m), whereas nanoelectronic characterization, including current mapping and I–V spectroscopy, was obtained in PF-TUNA (tunneling current) mode with a solid platinum RNM25PT300B probe (spring constant 18 N/m). Imaging scans were acquired at 1 Hz, and all I–V curves were collected under a compliance current of 100 pA to prevent damage to both tip and sample. The onset potential (VON) was defined as the voltage at which the measured current first exceeded the system noise level (≈ 3 pA).

## Paper

## Abstract

Grain boundaries (GBs) in insulating crystal films generally create lattice reconstruction and excess mid-gap states, which may form the transport pathways of charge carriers and lead to serious degradation of insulating properties. Here, we reveal the inert electrical behaviors of GBs in polycrystalline inorganic molecular dielectric film attributed to its special van der Waals structure. Temperature-dependent electrical measurements and first-principles calculations uncovered that such GBs are free of mid-gap states, which explains the unexpectedly low leakage current of Sb2O3 polycrystalline thin film. Through systematic measurements by conductive atomic force microscopy, we further verify the undistinguishable electrical behaviors within grains and at GBs of the polycrystalline film. Our findings may lay a solid foundation for the applications of inorganic molecular film as a compatible gate dielectric in advanced two-dimensional devices.

---

## Introduction

Insulating crystals with van der Waals (vdW) surface, such as hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) are gaining increasing attention for their superior performance as gate dielectrics, which facilitates the research in solid-state physics1–7 and integrated devices based on two-dimensional (2D) materials8–10. When integrated with 2D materials, they can form a well-saturated interface and enable the fabrication of high-performance devices such as field-effect transistors (FETs). However, most reported vdW insulating crystals with layered structure are integrated with 2D materials via the exfoliation-and-transfer method, incompatible with the semiconductor manufacturing processes11–17. A new type of vdW insulating crystal, antimony trioxide (Sb2O3) with a caged inorganic molecular structure, known as an inorganic molecular crystal (IMC), emerged and attracted plenty of research interests18–28. Apart from its excellent performance in 2D devices, it can be fabricated via thermal sublimation process. This foundry-compatible fabrication technique offers unparalleled convenience for the scalable integration of 2D circuits18,19. A puzzling fact, however, remains unexplained for this inorganic molecular dielectric film. A polycrystalline film usually possesses far inferior properties to its single-crystalline counterpart due to the presence of grain boundaries (GBs). For instance, GBs in insulators can create reconstructed lattice bonds and excess mid-gap states, which may act as charge carrier pathways and lead to serious degradation of their insulating performance29–37. Contrary to this classic theory, the fabricated polycrystalline inorganic molecular film (PIMF) of Sb2O3 with nanometer-scale grains exhibits an unexpectedly high insulating property18.

In this work, we present theoretical and experimental results on the electrical behaviors of Sb2O3 PIMF. The common GBs in conventional dielectric crystals can result in lattice reconstruction and excess mid-gap states, which form leakage pathways of charge carriers and degrade the insulating performance (Fig. 1a). We show, in contrast, that the excellent insulating properties of PIMF arise from the inert electrical behaviors of its GBs with a typical vdW structure. The saturated vdW GBs are free of mid-gap states, resulting in almost identical insulating properties of polycrystalline film and its single-crystal counterpart (Fig. 1b).

---

## Results

Fabrication of PIMF and electrical measurements
The PIMF of Sb2O3 can be fabricated via a thermal sublimation evaporation deposition method18,20. The deposited molecules remain in the cage-like structure and grow into a polycrystalline film on any given substrate, as illustrated in Fig. 2a. We first demonstrate the polycrystalline structure of the Sb2O3 film with a thickness of 10 nm grown on substrates of few-layer graphene (see Methods for details). This is the minimum thickness necessary to prevent the direct tunneling of charges18. As shown in Fig. 2b, the selected area electron diffraction (SAED) pattern confirms the single-crystalline nature of the underlying graphene, whereas the multi-oriented Sb2O3 domains give rise to grain size of around 9.6 nm (see Figure S1), close to the film thickness of 10 nm. This result implies that there may exist high-density transverse GBs (crossing from the top of the film to the bottom) within the film. For electrical characterizations, the Sb2O3 film was directly on a degenerately doped Si substrate, which serves as a flat bottom electrode. We tried to observe the Sb2O3 grains GBs from the cross-section HR-TEM image (Fig. 2d). We can clearly identify the Sb2O3 grains as well as the transverse GBs. Such an insulating film with a large number of continuous pathways for charge carrier transport is theoretically expected to possess a poor current-blocking property. In contrast, it exhibits a low leakage current in our device measurements at room temperature using a parallel plate capacitor (Figure S2). The current density (J) as a function of electric field (E) is furthermore investigated at various temperatures (Fig. 2e). We estimate that each device contains over 108 grains on average between the two electrodes with an area of 200 μm × 200 μm. Despite the presence of such high-density GBs, the measured leakage current density remains as low as 10−7 A/cm2 at an electrical field of 2 MV/cm. Moreover, as we can see in Fig. 2e, the measured leakage current density at varying electric field is independent of temperature. We analyze the electrical properties using Fowler-Nordheim tunneling (FNT) theory for a 10 nm thick insulating film at high electric field. The current density J and bias voltage V can be related using the following equation38–41:

ln(J/V2) = ln(q3m/8πhФB d2m*) - (8π(2m*)1/2 ФB3/2 d / 3hqV) (1)

where m and m* are electron mass and effective electron mass, q is electron charge, ФB is energy barrier, d is the thickness of the insulating layer. The strong linearity between ln(J(V))/V2 and 1/V can be identified from the plots (Fig. 4e inset), and they also exhibit clear independence on temperature, which is in good agreement with FNT theory. For an insulating layer with mid-gap states, the tunneling current generally follows the defect-assisted or trap-assisted tunneling theories42,43. For instance, the charge carriers tunneling assisted by the trap states located within the insulating layer may follow the Poole-Frenkel emission mechanism42,44,45. Its current density J and bias voltage V are related as:

ln(J(V)) / V ~ 1/V1/2 + 1/kT (2)

where kb is the Boltzmann constant and T is the temperature. We can see that for such a mechanism, ln(J(V))/V shows linear relation with V1/2 instead of V and it, moreover, exhibits clear dependence on temperature T45,46. These characteristics are in clear contrast to our measured results (Fig. 2e). Based on such analysis on the electrical transport behaviors, it can be, in turn, confirmed that the tunneling behaviors through our Sb2O3 insulating layer are free of defect- or trap-assisted mechanisms.

Impact of vdW GBs on DOS by calculations
We now try to gain insights into the impact of GBs on the electronic band structure of Sb2O3 crystals. As the molecular structure of Sb2O3 is preserved intact in the sublimation-deposition process, we reasonably assume that all the GBs in Sb2O3 are of vdW structure, as schematically shown in Fig. 2a. In order to investigate the impact of such GB presence on the insulating properties, we performed first-principles calculations to study the band structure of the Sb2O3 polycrystalline film (see details in supplementary materials). We constructed several typical crystal models with low-index crystal planes of (100), (110), (111), and (210), which have the lowest formation energy. A large enough vacuum layer is constructed to create the surface. In these crystal models, the complete molecular structure of Sb2O3 is maintained on the exposed surfaces (Fig. 3a). Since the possible excess mid-gap states in polycrystalline film originate from the breakage of the periodic crystal structure at the GBs, the band structure of our crystal models can represent the scenario of polycrystalline film47. Their calculated results of DOS are compared with those of bulk single crystal (Fig. 3b). The results show that they possess exactly the same band gap and introduce no excess mid-gap states for all the constructed crystal models, thanks to the termination of complete molecules. We specifically indicated that the DOS contributed from the top-layer exposed molecules, and all of their electronic states also remain out of the band gap (Fig. 3b). More explicitly, we constructed some representative crystal models containing GBs and investigated their DOS (see details in Supplementary Materials). For a face-centered cubic (FCC) crystal of Sb2O3, Σ3 and Σ5 twin GBs are preferentially formed in experiments due to their relatively low GB formation energies, which are chosen as two typical bi-crystal models for studying the effects of GBs. The Σ3 out-of-plane twist twin boundary (denoted as GB1, Fig. 3c) and the Σ5 in-plane tilt twin boundary (denoted as GB2, Fig. S3) were therefore selected as representative computational models due to their relatively small number of atoms. They can effectively balance computational efficiency and the accurate description of their physical properties. Their crystal structures were optimized, and electronic structures were calculated (Fig. 3d). The two bi-crystal models possess very similar band gap, which is slightly smaller than the bulk crystal calculated via the same approximation method (see detailed analysis in Supplementary Materials). No excess mid-gap states are created despite the presence of GBs. Such theoretical results imply that the presence of vdW GBs in Sb2O3 PIMF will not result in any mid-gap states, in clear contrast to conventional oxide dielectric materials30,31. The PIMF Sb2O3 possesses an identical band gap to the single-crystal film.

Electrical measurement of Grains and GBs in PIMF via C-AFM
To directly investigate the insulating properties of PIMF at GBs, we employ conductive atomic force microscopy (C-AFM) to probe the nanoelectronic properties of Sb2O3 PIMF at the GBs and within the grains (see experimental details in supplementary materials). C-AFM allows for electrical measurements at local positions with nanometer resolution, and the results can be conveniently correlated with the morphology of the sample surface48–51, enabling us to access the electrical behaviors of GBs and grains simultaneously (Fig. 4a). We first obtain the morphology of the PIMF. Thanks to the effect of GB grooving in the film that grows via deposition, we can identify the GBs and grains from the AFM images (Fig. 4b). We then apply ramp voltage stress on specific positions (at GBs or in grains) and carry out the electrical measurements. Figure 4c shows the forward and backwards sweeping E-I curves obtained at GBs and within grains from over 100 positions, with a current limitation of 100 pA to protect the tip and the sample52. Statistically, we find no discernible difference between GBs and grains' E-I curves. The average E-I curves obtained from GBs and grains are almost overlapped (thick curves in Fig. 4c), both for forward and backwards sweeping, which implies an identical electrical property for GBs and grains of our Sb2O3 PIMF. We also analyzed the average E-I curves using FNT theory, as shown in Fig. 4d. Their linear relation implies that both the electrical behaviors of GBs and grains are in good agreement with the FNT as well (analysis of the measured data is shown in Fig. S3). The required electrical field to reach a fixed leakage current of 3 pA for GBs and grains is plotted statically in Fig. 4e, from which we can see that they exhibit very similar values. C-AFM also allows for mapping leakage currents over a given area, which can provide the insulating properties over a continuous area. Applying a constant bias voltage of 3.5 V on the C-AFM tip, the leakage currents in a 500 nm × 500 nm area are mapped for three times (Fig. 4f). As we can observe, most area exhibits an ultra-low conductivity while some regions are more conductive (dark points in Fig. 4f), however, it is clear that such highly-conductive regions do not correlate to the positions of GBs and the position do not repeat in multiple scans; moreover, the currents decrease as the stress proceed due to the presence of charge trapping effect, i.e. some charges get trapped and released from the trapping points. This result is in contrast with multiple observations of enhanced currents and fast degradation at the grain boundaries of metal oxides like HfO253,54. Therefore, this behavior observed in GBs of Sb2O3 PIMF is quite unique and offers higher opportunities for being used as a gate dielectric.

---

## Methods

Thermal evaporation deposition of PIMF Sb2O3
The deposition of Sb2O3 was carried out in a standard thermal evaporation deposition system (Nexdep, Angstrom Engineering) in a high vacuum (10−6 torr). Sb2O3 powder was sublimated by heating and deposited on substrates. The deposition rate was precisely controlled by an in-situ quartz crystal oscillator. To maintain the flatness of the obtained Sb2O3 film, the deposition rate in this work was 0.06 Å s−1 for the entire fabrication process.

Sample preparation for TEM characterizations
For plan-view TEM samples, we exfoliated a few-layer graphene flakes onto SiO2/Si substrate and then transferred them onto a TEM grid assisted by a PMMA membrane. Then the PMMA membrane on the TEM grid is dissolved in acetone. Afterwards, the TEM grid with graphene flakes is annealed in an Ar atmosphere to remove the PMMA residues on graphene flakes, which is then loaded into the thermal evaporation deposition system, and Sb2O3 is deposited. For the cross-section TEM lamella, 10 nm of Sb2O3 was deposited onto a degenerately doped silicon substrate, and then the lamella was fabricated by a dual focused ion beam system (Helios Nanolab G3 UC, FEI). TEM images and SAED were obtained using an FEI Tecnai G2 20.

Preparation and characterization of capacitor devices
10 nm of Sb2O3 was deposited onto a degenerately doped silicon substrate. A shadow mask with a predefined size of 200 μm × 200 μm was placed over the film, followed by the deposition of 40 nm of Au via thermal evaporation to form the top metal electrode. In such a way, the devices for electrical characterizations can be maintained free of contamination resulting from the fabrication processes.

Electrical measurements
Current-voltage measurements were performed in a probe station (Lakeshore) equipped with a semiconductor analyzer (Keithley 4200). We pump the chamber and keep it in a high vacuum (10−6 torr) for 3 h to eliminate the gas adsorption on device surfaces before the device test. Afterwards, the device tests are carried out at various temperatures.

Theoretical calculations
The details of the theoretical calculations are described in the Supplementary Materials.

C-AFM characterization
Conductive atomic force microscopy (C-AFM) experiments were carried out on a Bruker Dimension Icon instrument fitted with a Nanoscope VI controller and PFTUNA module. Measurements were performed in ambient air (relative humidity ≈ 54%). Surface topography was mapped in tapping mode using an NCHV-A tip (spring constant 42 N/m), whereas nanoelectronic characterization, including current mapping and I–V spectroscopy, was obtained in PF-TUNA (tunneling current) mode with a solid platinum RNM25PT300B probe (spring constant 18 N/m). Imaging scans were acquired at 1 Hz, and all I–V curves were collected under a compliance current of 100 pA to prevent damage to both tip and sample. The onset potential (VON) was defined as the voltage at which the measured current first exceeded the system noise level (≈ 3 pA).
